request: We want to notify the right people when a freelancer's mission is about to end.

problem.value: Mission ends are noticed too late or by nobody, so downstream actions (renewal or extension, final invoicing, validation, offboarding) are missed or rushed. The real need behind 'notify' is not yet stated.
problem.evidence: Request: 'notify the right people when a freelancer's mission is about to end.' The underlying pain is deduced from the Mission domain notes (end-of-mission is an event that triggers notifications, final invoicing and validation).

current_process.value: Unknown how mission ends are tracked today (manual follow-up, spreadsheet, memory, nothing).

existing_solutions.value: Unknown whether the platform already has a notification or reminder mechanism (e.g. the role-based notifications used in approval circuits) that could be reused or extended, or an unused feature or tool already paid for.
existing_solutions.evidence: Not mentioned. The b2b-platform context lists role-based notifications as a key concept, so reuse is plausible.

success_metrics.value: Likely: no mission ends without the right people having been warned in time, and fewer late renewals or late final invoices. No target has been stated.

payer.value: Internal feature of an existing platform; the client or platform owner pays.
payer.evidence: b2b-platform context. This is not a product idea.

actors.value: The 'right people' are not defined. Candidates: the freelancer, the internal manager or mission owner, HR, the client's contacts (by role: billing, HR, operational), and an administrator. The platform's trigger is the system itself (scheduled).
actors.evidence: Request: 'the right people'. The candidate list comes from the context card: a Client has Contacts with roles, and notification routing depends on the contact role.

business_objects.value: Mission (start date, end date, linked to Freelancer and Client), Freelancer, Client and Contact (with role), Notification (event, recipient, channel, sent status).
business_objects.evidence: Domain notes: Mission is linked to a Freelancer and a Client and has a start and an end.

business_rules.value: Undefined: how far before the end counts as 'about to end' (e.g. 30, 15 or 7 days), whether there is one reminder or several, who receives which one, and whether the rule varies by client, contract or country.

workflow.value: Unknown whether the notification is informational only or starts a follow-up (extend the mission, confirm the end, trigger final invoicing or validation) and who acts on it. The trigger is presumably a scheduled check, so asynchronous.
workflow.evidence: Request is silent on what happens after the notification. The context card notes that end-of-mission can trigger final invoicing and validation.

integrations.value: Channel not specified (email, in-app, other), nor whether any external system is updated.
integrations.evidence: Request does not name a channel. The context card says 'notify' implies who, when and which channel.

permissions.value: A recipient should only be told about missions they are allowed to see (own client's missions, own team). Freelancer rate and contract data must not leak through the notification content.
permissions.evidence: Deduced from the context card: permissions and routing depend on contact role, and permissions are often forgotten until acceptance.

config_vs_custom.value: Unknown whether lead time, recipients and wording are standard for all clients or configurable per client. The context card says notification routing is client-specific.

constraints.value: GDPR applies to freelancer personal data in notifications. No deadline or dependencies have been stated.
constraints.evidence: Context card regulatory section. The request gives no deadline.

edge_cases.value: To settle: end date changed after the notification (extension, early end, cancellation), mission created or started with less than the lead time remaining, no end date set (open-ended), no contact with the right role, and the same notification being sent twice.
edge_cases.evidence: Deduced from the 'create X automatically' traps (trigger, idempotency, incomplete source data).

reporting.value: At most a log of what was sent to whom and when. No audit or compliance need has been named.
reporting.evidence: Nothing in the request suggests an audit requirement.

acceptance.value: Not defined. A first scenario would be: a mission ending in N days produces exactly one notification to each defined recipient, and an extended mission produces none or a corrected one.
acceptance.evidence: No acceptance criteria in the request.

risks.value: Risks: notifying the wrong person, spam from repeated reminders, missed notifications when a date changes, and existing missions needing a data backfill (missing end dates or contact roles).
risks.evidence: Deduced from the context card traps.

acquisition.value: Not applicable: this is a feature for existing platform users.

summary.objective: Automatically warn the relevant people shortly before a freelancer's mission ends, so that follow-up actions (renewal, final invoicing, validation) are not missed.
summary.scope: A scheduled, date-based notification tied to the Mission end event, routed to recipients by role (client contact roles, internal staff, possibly the freelancer) over one or more channels. Whether it is configurable per client, and whether it triggers further actions, is still open.
assumptions: This is an internal feature on the existing B2B platform, so there is no separate payer or acquisition question.
The trigger is a scheduled, asynchronous event ahead of the mission end date.
Recipients are probably determined by contact role (billing, operational, HR) plus internal staff.
The freelancer's personal data falls under GDPR, which affects who can see what.
The goal is that every mission end is flagged in time. No specific metric has been stated.
summary.blind_spot: 'The right people' and 'about to end' are both undefined. Behind them are two bigger questions: whether an existing notification mechanism can simply be reused, and whether the notification is only a message or must start an action such as renewal or final invoicing. Date changes, extensions and early ends can also cause duplicate or stale notifications.

briefs.problem: Freelancer mission ends are noticed late or by nobody, so renewal, final invoicing and validation are missed or rushed.
briefs.solution: A scheduled check on mission end dates that sends a de-duplicated notification to recipients routed by role, ahead of the end.
introduces: a scheduled job that scans mission end dates
recipient routing by internal role and client-contact role
idempotent notification tracking (one reminder per mission, per lead time, per recipient)
handling of end-date changes (extension, early end, cancellation)

challenges.headline: Build before checking reuse
challenges.premise: A new mission-end notification feature must be built.
challenges.alternative: The platform already uses role-based notifications in its approval circuits. Registering mission end as one more event on that mechanism could replace most of a new build.
challenges.consequence: A separate notification path duplicates routing, templates and permission checks, and then has to be maintained beside the existing one.
challenges.recommendation: Inspect the existing notification mechanism and decide reuse versus build before estimating.

challenges.headline: Heads-up versus actionable prompt
challenges.premise: A notification alone solves the problem.
challenges.alternative: The pain is missed follow-up (extension, final invoicing, validation). A notification that links to the mission and the next action addresses that. A bare reminder may be read and still forgotten.
challenges.consequence: Building only a reminder risks delivering something that changes nothing. Adding actions later reshapes the workflow and permissions.
challenges.recommendation: Ask what goes wrong today when nobody sees the end coming, and decide whether v1 is heads-up only or heads-up plus a link to the follow-up.

complexity_reasons: scheduled, asynchronous trigger with no duplicate sends
recipient routing that depends on contact role
end dates that change after reminders have gone out
briefs.cost_driver: recipient routing and rule configuration (fixed versus per client)
risks: Notifying the wrong person, such as a client contact who should not see the freelancer's details, exposes rate or contract data and brings GDPR exposure.
Missions with no end date, or clients with no contact of the right role, may silently receive nothing; existing data may need a backfill.
Changed end dates can leave stale reminders pending or cause duplicates.
Repeated reminders create noise that users learn to ignore.
If the existing notification mechanism is coupled to approval circuits, extending it may affect shared modules.

opportunities.text: Generalize the role-based notification mechanism into a date-driven reminder engine that other date-based events can reuse.
Fire the same end-of-mission event for final invoicing and validation so they can subscribe to it later.

next_steps: Inspect the existing notification mechanism to decide reuse versus build.
Run a short session with the business owner to fix the recipients, the lead time and number of reminders, and whether v1 is heads-up only.
Decide whether the rules are standard for all clients or configurable, and size accordingly.
Define acceptance scenarios, including extended, cancelled and open-ended missions.

decisions.decision: The trigger is a scheduled, time-based check on the mission end date, so the notification is asynchronous.
decisions.why: Nothing happens at the moment a mission is about to end; the system must look ahead.
decisions.alternative: Event-driven triggers only on mission edits.
decisions.tradeoff: Needs scheduling and idempotency handling in exchange for catching missions that were never edited.

decisions.decision: Recipients are chosen by role, as notification routing is elsewhere on the platform.
decisions.why: Contacts already carry roles (billing, HR, operational) and routing by role is the platform's existing pattern.
decisions.tradeoff: Depends on contact data being complete, in exchange for correct routing.

Heads-up only versus actionable follow-up

page.title: Notifying the right people before a mission ends
page.recommendation: Decide first whether this is a simple heads-up or the start of a follow-up (extend, invoice, validate). We recommend a scheduled check on mission end dates that sends one de-duplicated notification per recipient, reusing the platform's existing role-based notifications if they can carry it, and linking to the mission so the next step is one click away.
page.why: Your request names the recipients and timing only as 'the right people' and 'about to end', so the real value is in preventing missed follow-up, not in the message itself. Reusing what the platform already does for approvals is likely the cheapest route, and routing by contact role keeps the right information with the right person.
page.cost_and_risk: The main effort is routing recipients by role and, if clients want their own rules, configuring lead time, recipients and wording per client. The risk that matters most is telling the wrong person, which could expose freelancer rates or personal data, followed by stale or repeated reminders when end dates change.

open.question: Who exactly should be notified: the freelancer, the internal owner, HR, and/or client contacts (and which contact role)?
open.would_change: Client contacts add role-based routing and data-exposure rules; internal-only recipients make it much smaller.

open.question: What should the notification lead to, and what goes wrong today when nobody sees the end coming?
open.would_change: A heads-up only is a small build; a prompt that opens renewal or final invoicing is a larger one.

open.question: How many days before the end, and how many reminders? Is it the same for every client?
open.would_change: Per-client variation turns a fixed schedule into configuration with settings and defaults.

open.question: Does the platform already have a reminder or notification mechanism, or a paid tool, that we should reuse?
open.would_change: If yes, much of the build disappears; if not, a dedicated notification path must be built.

assumptions.text: The trigger is a scheduled check against the mission end date, not a manual action.
Notification routing follows contact roles, as elsewhere on the platform.
No audit or compliance requirement exists beyond a log of what was sent.
GDPR applies to freelancer data shown in notifications.

briefs.problem: A freelancer's mission can end without the people who must renew, hand over, invoice or validate having been warned in time.
briefs.solution: A scheduled check on mission end dates that sends role-based notices ahead of the end, ideally by reusing the platform's existing notification mechanism.
introduces: a scheduled job that evaluates mission end dates and fires notices ahead of them
role-based recipient resolution from client contact roles and internal staff
idempotent notice tracking, so the same reminder is not sent twice
re-evaluation when a mission end date is extended, shortened or cancelled
a notification record of who was told and when (if confirmed as needed)

challenges.headline: Build before checking for reuse
challenges.premise: A new mission-end notification feature has to be built.
challenges.alternative: The platform already treats end-of-mission as an event and has role-based notifications as a core concept. Configuring an existing reminder mechanism, such as the one used for contracts or leave, with a new trigger and recipient rule may cover most of the need.
challenges.consequence: Building a separate scheduler and notice engine duplicates logic and adds a second place where routing and permission rules must be maintained.
challenges.recommendation: Inspect the existing notification and reminder capabilities before estimating any build.

challenges.headline: Notification versus the real need
challenges.premise: Warning people is enough to stop mission ends from causing problems.
challenges.alternative: If the pain is a missed renewal, a late final invoice or a skipped validation, the notice could carry a direct link to the next action. Alternatively, a plain heads-up is enough if the follow-up is already handled elsewhere.
challenges.consequence: A purely informational alert may be ignored or acted on outside the system. An action-starting alert is a larger build with its own states and permissions.
challenges.recommendation: Name the specific failure this prevents with the client and decide whether the first release is informational only.

challenges.headline: Undefined 'right people'
challenges.premise: Recipients can be worked out as 'the right people' without being specified.
challenges.alternative: Define recipients by contact role (operational, billing, HR, internal manager), with a fallback when a role has no valid contact. This depends on the existing directory data being complete.
challenges.consequence: Gaps in contact roles in existing data mean missed notices, while over-broad routing sends notices about freelancers (personal data) to people who should not see them.
challenges.recommendation: Agree a recipient-by-role table and audit how many existing missions have the required contacts before launch.

complexity_reasons: recipient routing by contact role and permission scope
briefs.cost_driver: recipient routing and timing rules, unless an existing notification engine can be reused
risks: Incomplete contact roles in existing client data cause missed or misrouted notices.
Duplicate or stale reminders if end dates change after a notice was sent and re-evaluation is not handled.
Rolling out on existing missions can trigger a burst of notices on missions already inside the window unless a no-retroactive-notice rule is set.
Freelancer personal data in notices is subject to GDPR, so message content and recipients need care.
Notification and permission rules are shared across modules, so a change may touch several screens.

opportunities.text: Express this as a generic 'date-approaching' reminder rule (event, lead time, recipient roles) that other date-driven events can reuse.
Link the end-of-mission notice to the next action, such as extension or final invoicing, in a later phase.

next_steps: Check what notification or reminder mechanism the platform already has and whether it can carry a mission-end trigger.
Run a short session with the client to fix the failure being prevented, the recipient roles and the lead time(s).
Audit existing missions for end-date and contact-role completeness, and decide the rollout rule for missions already near their end.
Estimate and build an informational first release on the confirmed rules, and defer per-client configuration and action links until demanded.

decisions.decision: The trigger is time-based, evaluated on a schedule rather than inline.
decisions.why: A mission ending soon is a date condition, not a user action, so nothing happens at the moment of notice that the user waits on.
decisions.alternative: Inline checks when a mission is viewed or edited.
decisions.tradeoff: Delivery is eventual rather than immediate, and reminders need idempotency, in exchange for notices that do not depend on anyone opening the mission.

decisions.decision: Recipients are chosen by contact role rather than one address per client.
decisions.why: Contacts already carry roles on this platform, and routing frequently depends on them.
decisions.tradeoff: Depends on the quality of role data, in exchange for the right person being told.

page.title: Mission-end notices: reuse before building
page.recommendation: Decide whether this is a new build or a configuration of what the platform already has. We recommend first checking the existing notification capability, then delivering a first release that only informs: a scheduled notice sent to defined roles ahead of the mission end date.
page.why: Your request names the outcome, warning the right people, but not who they are, how early to warn them, or what they must do next. The platform already treats the end of a mission as an event and routes notices by contact role, so reuse could remove most of the build. An informational first release keeps cost and risk low while the rules are settled.
page.cost_and_risk: The main cost is the recipient and timing rules: routing by contact role, scheduling, and avoiding duplicate or stale reminders when an end date changes. The risk that matters most is incomplete contact data on existing missions, which causes missed notices or notices sent to the wrong people.

open.question: Does the platform already have a reminder or notification mechanism, for example for contracts or leave, that could carry this?
open.would_change: If yes, this becomes mostly configuration and the estimate drops sharply; if no, a scheduler and notice engine must be built.

open.question: Who exactly should be told (client operational or billing contact, internal manager or HR, the freelancer), and does the message differ by role?
open.would_change: Determines the routing model and the permission scope of each notice.

open.question: How many days before the end should people be warned, with one reminder or several, and should reminders restart if the end date changes?
open.would_change: Sets the scheduler design and the handling of date changes and duplicates.

open.question: What goes wrong today when a mission ends unannounced, and is a warning enough or should it start an action such as renewal or final invoicing?
open.would_change: If the notice must start an action, the first release is larger than an informational alert.

open.question: Should the timing, recipients and wording be the same for all clients or configurable per client?
open.would_change: Per-client rules require a configuration model and admin screens rather than one fixed rule.

assumptions.text: Notices are triggered by time, a set number of days before the end date, on a schedule.
Recipients are chosen by contact role and only hear about missions within their own scope.
This is an internal platform feature with no external vendor or separate payer.
Missions with no end date, extended or cancelled missions, and duplicate notices need explicit rules.

briefs.problem: Nobody is reliably warned before a freelancer's mission ends, so renewal, final invoicing and validation are missed or late.
briefs.solution: A scheduled, date-based notification ahead of each mission's end, routed to recipients by their role, with an optional follow-up action.
introduces: a scheduled job that scans upcoming mission end dates
role-based recipient resolution using client contact roles and internal staff
duplicate protection and recalculation when an end date changes
a notification log of who was told what and when
a lead-time and recipient configuration, if clients differ

challenges.headline: Build before checking existing tools
challenges.premise: A new notification mechanism has to be built for mission ends.
challenges.alternative: The platform already treats role-based notifications as a concept. Extending that mechanism, or switching on a licensed reminder or workflow tool, could cover most of this with a new trigger and a recipient rule.
challenges.consequence: A parallel notification path duplicates channels, preferences and permission checks, and it has to be maintained separately from the existing one.
challenges.recommendation: Inventory the platform's current notification capability and any licensed but unused tool before estimating any build.

challenges.headline: Message or workflow?
challenges.premise: Notifying people is the goal, as if a message alone prevents missed follow-up.
challenges.alternative: If the real aim is renewal, final invoicing or validation, the notification can carry a link to the action, or create a task, with a simple acknowledged or not state. A pure message with no trace is cheaper but cannot show that anyone acted.
challenges.consequence: Building only a message may leave the missed-follow-up problem unsolved. Building a full workflow by default multiplies the scope.
challenges.recommendation: Settle with the client what must happen after the notification, and build the smallest version that covers it.

challenges.headline: One undefined 'right people'
challenges.premise: The right recipients are obvious and can be derived from the mission alone.
challenges.alternative: Resolving recipients by the client contact's role, with a named internal fallback when no contact has that role, makes the routing explicit and testable.
challenges.consequence: Without a fallback, a client with no contact in the right role silently receives nothing. Notifying the wrong contact exposes the freelancer's personal data under GDPR.
challenges.recommendation: Agree a recipient-by-role table and a fallback rule with the client before build.

complexity_reasons: scheduled asynchronous trigger with duplicate protection
cancelling or recalculating reminders when an end date changes
risks: Reminders sent for missions that were extended, ended early or cancelled, because pending notifications are not recalculated.
Duplicate notifications when the scheduled job reruns or a mission changes.
Freelancer personal data reaching a contact who should not see it, under GDPR.
Missions already past or near their end date when the feature goes live, producing a burst of late notices.
A parallel notification path built next to an existing one, doubling maintenance.

opportunities.text: Make the date-based trigger plus role-based recipient resolution a reusable component, so other date events can use it.
Reuse the same engine for contract end and renewal reminders.

next_steps: Inventory the existing notification capability and any licensed unused tool, then decide to reuse or build.
Workshop with the client to fix the recipients by role, the fallback, the lead times and what must happen after the notification.
Specify how date changes, extensions and early ends affect pending reminders, and the go-live handling of missions already near their end.
Build the smallest version: one scheduled reminder, role-based routing, and a log of who was notified.

decisions.decision: The notification is driven by a scheduled, asynchronous trigger on the mission end date.
decisions.why: A date-based reminder fires without a user waiting on it, so queued delivery with retries fits.
decisions.alternative: An inline trigger when a user edits the mission.
decisions.tradeoff: A window where the notification state can lag the mission data, in exchange for dependable delivery.

decisions.decision: Recipients are resolved by contact role rather than a fixed list.
decisions.why: The platform already attaches roles to client contacts, and routing depends on them.
decisions.alternative: A fixed list of addresses per client.
decisions.tradeoff: Needs a fallback when no contact has the role, but avoids manual list upkeep.

page.title: Mission-end notification: reuse or build?
page.recommendation: Decide first whether this can be delivered by extending the notification capability you already have. We recommend a scheduled reminder ahead of each mission's end, sent to recipients chosen by contact role with a named fallback, and we advise confirming what follows the notification before building anything more than that.
page.why: Your request is to warn the right people, but it does not say who they are, how early, or what they should do next. The platform already uses role-based notifications and client contacts carry roles, so reuse may cover most of the work. Settling these points first avoids building a message that does not prevent missed renewals or late final invoices.
page.cost_and_risk: The main effort is routing recipients correctly and keeping reminders accurate when an end date changes, is extended or ends early. The risk that matters most is a wrong or duplicate notification, which can also expose the freelancer's personal data to the wrong contact.

open.question: Is the notification only informational, or must someone act on it or acknowledge it?

assumptions.text: This is an internal feature of the existing platform, with no separate payer.
The trigger is scheduled and asynchronous, ahead of the mission end date.
Recipients are chosen by client contact role plus internal staff, and possibly the freelancer.
Success means no mission ends without the right people having been warned in time.
